```{=html}
<p class="lede">A free, hands-on course in modern natural language processing —
written for engineers and statisticians who don't have a computer-science
background, and taken from a live course at METU (ODTÜ), Ankara.</p>
<p class="meta">Interactive · Open source · Updated as the field moves
<span class="dot">•</span> English now, Türkçe soon</p>
<div class="btn-row">
  <a class="btn btn-anlp-primary" href="chapters/01-why-nlp-now.html">Start reading →</a>
  <a class="btn btn-anlp-ghost" href="https://github.com/bbardakk/metu-applied-nlp">Star on GitHub</a>
</div>
```
:::

The title above is not decoration — it is the book's first lesson. That is
roughly how a language model actually reads: text is [split into subword
tokens]{.hl}, and everything else — embeddings, attention, generation — is
built on top of that stream. By the end of this book you will know exactly
what happens to those chips, and you will have built working systems on top
of models that process them.

Thirty-nine chapters is the destination, not the current state. Chapters
marked ⚡ ship with working in-browser widgets; the rest are being drafted in
order, and the [changelog](#updates) records each one as it lands.

## How this book works

**It assumes statistics, not CS.** If you can read a regression table, you
have every prerequisite. New machinery is introduced by analogy to things you
already know — attention is a [learned weighted average]{.hl}, embeddings are
coordinates, fine-tuning is re-estimation.

**It is interactive.** Key ideas come with widgets that run entirely in your
browser — drag a temperature slider, watch a probability distribution reshape
itself. No installation, no GPU. Start with the
[attention head explorer](chapters/07-transformers.qmd), then the
[sampling policy explorer](chapters/18-decoding-structured-output.qmd).

**It is executable.** Code chapters ship as real, runnable Python. Every
chapter links its notebook so you can open it in Colab and break things.

**It is alive.** The field moves; the book moves with it. Watch the
repository or subscribe to the changelog to see what changed between visits.
Found an error? Every page has an *Edit* link — fixes arrive as pull requests.

## For instructors

The book is deliberately larger than one semester. A 13–14 week course fits
comfortably as Parts I–IV plus a selection from Part V; Parts V–VII are built
so an agents-focused or production-focused second course can be cut from the
same material. Slides, homework notebooks, and a suggested grading scheme are
being added chapter by chapter. Everything is CC BY 4.0: reuse it, translate
it, remix it — just keep the attribution.

## Updates

| Date | Change |
|------|--------|
| 2026-08 | Chapter 13 *Sequence Labeling and Information Extraction* drafted — NER on WikiANN Turkish, and an audit of the benchmark before any of it. **13.06% of its test set is byte-identical to a training sentence**, and the leakage bonus falls monotonically with how much a system memorises: +26.50 span F1 for a gazetteer, +16.25 for a CRF, +7.65 for a fine-tuned encoder — which makes that gap a usable measurement of how much of a score is recall rather than generalisation. A dictionary scores 55.26, an eighteen-second CPU CRF scores 85.45, and BERTurk needs 2,000–5,000 labelled sentences to pass it, reaching 91.92 on all 20,000; at 200 sentences it scores **3.14** and has learned only to say `O`. Illegal BIO transitions turn out to be learned away rather than prevented — 3,739 half-trained, 139 at full budget, never zero, against a CRF's structural zero. Zero-shot LLM extraction reaches 60.57 with no labels and is 1,200× slower. And `ollama` 0.24.0 silently ignores a JSON schema on `/api/chat` while enforcing it on `/api/generate`. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 12 *Text Classification* drafted — the chapter 4 split, recovered rather than re-drawn by matching a vectoriser fingerprint of 101,659 dimensions across four candidate constructions. Moving one threshold beat every resampling method (77.66 against 76.09 for class weights, 74.72 for SMOTE) and class weighting multiplied calibration error by 3.6×. Ten local-LLM runs put the prompted-versus-fine-tuned crossover at **2,000 labels**, where the two tie to 0.08 macro-F1 points (p = 0.97) — below that the prompt wins by 8.79, above it the encoder wins by 4.73, and the encoder classifies a document 142× cheaper. Prompt-language and few-shot folklore held for weak models and vanished into noise for strong ones. One run scored 93.75% accuracy by being completely broken: a reasoning model spent its 24-token budget inside a `thinking` field the parser never read, and every unparseable answer fell through to the majority class. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 11 *Similarity, Clustering and Topic Discovery* drafted — the chapter 4 corpus again, with the labels locked away until the last section. Clustering never recovers sentiment: the best adjusted Rand index anywhere is 0.0083, the internal indices pick 50, 4 and 2 clusters, and HDBSCAN never returns more than three clusters at any setting, on 53–100% noise. It does find a shipping Unicode bug nobody was looking for — `"TAVSİYE".lower()` splits into two tokens, and one k-means cluster is 94.7% affected against a 6.0% background — and reading 13.3% of the corpus surfaces 56.0% of its complaints. The metric that ranked the tokenizer debris highest was topic coherence. |
| 2026-08 | Part III widened from three chapters to six, taking the book to 39. Similarity, clustering and topic discovery now sits before classification, because the honest first move on a new corpus is to find its structure rather than to start labelling it; summarization and machine translation give generation tasks a home of their own. Chapters after Part III shifted by three. Cross-references are anchors rather than numbers, so nothing else moved. |
| 2026-08 | Book restructured from 13 chapters in 4 parts to 36 in 7: Core NLP Tasks, Agentic Systems, and Agents in Production are now full parts rather than single chapters, and the capstone is a chapter of its own. Sampling and decoding moved out of the transformers chapter into their own chapter, taking the temperature/top-k/top-p explorer with them. Existing chapters keep their content and their cross-references; only the numbering moved. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 10 *Reasoning Models and Test-Time Compute* drafted — a thinking-budget sweep on Qwen3 where 6.74× the tokens bought exactly zero accuracy points and no budget was statistically separable from no-thinking at 200 questions. Self-consistency had the right answer in the sample 85.8% of the time and voted it out down to 76.7%. A planted wrong answer sent 71% of the damage to answers that were neither right nor planted, and the faithfulness detector had to be measured before its output could be believed. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 9 *Post-Training: Adaptation and Alignment* drafted — LoRA on BERTurk, seven runs on one laptop GPU on the chapter 4 split. Rank 1, at 0.035% of the weights, takes a frozen encoder from 48.37 to 80.47 macro-F1 and clears the tf-idf baseline; rank 64 is worse than rank 8. The full fine-tune wins macro-F1 and loses accuracy to every LoRA run, which turns out to be a product decision rather than a training one. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 8 *Pretraining and the Model Landscape* drafted — where the data comes from, what a run costs, and six real tokenizers measured on 1,157 aligned English–Turkish sentence pairs. Turkish costs 1.23× its English translation on Llama 3 and 1.98× on GPT-2, while a Turkish-native tokenizer inverts the penalty to 0.58×. Also why the most aggressive deduplication in an open corpus made the data worse. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 7 *Transformers and Attention* drafted — self-attention built from the weighted-average intuition upward, with every number of one layer computed by hand for a three-token Turkish sentence, seven architecture diagrams, and fifteen interactive controls. Multi-head attention, RoPE and ALiBi, encoder/decoder masking, KV cache and GQA arithmetic, mixture of experts, and scaling laws. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 6 *Language Models: From N-grams to Neural Networks* drafted — the pair of sentences chapter 4 could not tell apart, now separated by a bigram model. Kneser-Ney reaches 333.5 test perplexity and a neural LM 332.4, a tie that hides everything: the n-gram model copies 91.6% of what it generates and the neural model copies none of it. The chapter is where the bet on neural models gets placed, and it says so. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 5 *Data, Annotation, and Ground Truth* drafted — the same corpus and split as chapter 4, with only the labels varying. A 2% error rate in the *test* labels reverses the chapter 4 leaderboard, 1,000 clean labels beat 40,000 at 10% noise, and 40% noise into the majority class costs nothing while 1% into the minority costs more than a full representation upgrade. Half of the model's confident mistakes turn out to be texts a binary label cannot express. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 4 *A Representation Bake-Off* drafted — every method from chapters 2 and 3 run against 40,000 Turkish product reviews on one split with one classifier. Tf-idf wins by ten macro-F1 points, fastText fixes out-of-vocabulary completely without helping accuracy at all, and the learning curve shows exactly where that verdict flips. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 3 *Embeddings* drafted — PPMI and SVD by hand, skip-gram with negative sampling written from scratch in NumPy, GloVe, fastText on Turkish morphology, doc2vec against the chapter 2 baseline, and four interactive explorers. Every number measured, including the ones that make embeddings look bad. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 2 *Text as Data* drafted — how a word becomes a vector, worked BPE and TF-IDF code with real outputs, four interactive explorers, plus intuition checks and interview questions. |
| 2026-08 | Chapter 1 *Why NLP, Why Now* drafted — an interactive seventy-year timeline and a "where does your field meet NLP" explorer. Turkish translation published alongside it. |
| 2026-08 | Book skeleton published: 12 chapters, 3 appendices, 2 interactive explorers. |
